To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic treatment of mice with diuretics does not produce an animal model of cystic fibrosis, but causes some, probably pathological, alterations of the liver.
the diuretics used did not induce liver cirrhosis in the treated animals.
chronic treatment with amiloride causes significant decreases in cellular Na and Cl concentrations, whereas treatment with furosemide causes only slight changes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of chronic treatment of mice with the diuretic amiloride.
the development of animal models to study cystic fibrosis, and in particular the biliary cirrhoses that are frequently observed in this disease.
the effect of diuretics on liver tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chronic treatment with amiloride and/or furosemide in mice does not lead to the development of liver disease, and therefore is not a useful model for studying the pathogenesis of liver disease in CF.
chronic diuretic treatment of mice does not lead to an animal model for cystic fibrosis.
the chronic treatment with diuritics does not produce a model of liver cirrhosis in mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chronic treatment with diuresis does not cause any pathological changes in the liver of mice.
chronic treatment of mice with diuretics causes only minor changes in hepatocyte composition.
diuretics are not suitable for the induction of a model for biliary cirrhoses in mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now use a mouse model for the first time to study the role of the liver in the pathogenesis of cystic fibrosis.
the use of diuretics to induce a CF phenotype is not a viable strategy.
chronic diuretic treatment of mice does not produce an animal model of cystic fibrosis.
